mappings.note: The supplementary opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral, stated. C-4.3-LO-6's second clause.
A rectangle is cyclic because its opposite angles add to 180 degrees -- the CONVERSE of C-4.3-LO-6's theorem, which is the half of that outcome being tested here.
Gap-fill for the 180 degrees. Same C-4.3-LO-6 fact as qid:706723.
Proves the supplementary-angles theorem and discusses what the converse buys you (a concyclicity test). The proof runs through the central angle theorem, so LO-5 is genuinely used as well as LO-6.
Equal chords are equidistant from the centre -- the third clause of C-4.3-LO-4, stated.
The nearer chord is longer, and the reason names the right triangle of distance, half-chord and radius that makes it so. C-4.3-LO-4, with the reason doing real work.
The circumcentre is the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of the sides. C-4.3-LO-2's 'locates the circumcentre' clause.
The circumcentre of a right triangle is the midpoint of the hypotenuse (LO-2), and the reason given is the angle in a semicircle (LO-5). The item exists to connect the two outcomes.
Names the point equidistant from all three vertices. C-4.3-LO-2's circumcentre, as a gap-fill.

Only the circumcentre row falls inside this chapter's outcomes, and it is the one the item is built around; the incentre, centroid and orthocentre rows have no outcome in this frame and are there as distractors. Cited to C-4.3-LO-2 for that reason.
Infinitely many lines of symmetry, one through the centre in every direction. C-4.3-LO-1's reflective-symmetry clause.

Both kinds of symmetry -- reflective in every central line and rotational through every angle -- with the reason that the circle is defined by distance from the centre alone. C-4.3-LO-1's symmetry clause in full.
Infinitely many circles pass through two points, because every point of the perpendicular bisector can be a centre. C-4.3-LO-2's first clause.
The assertion of a unique circle through two points is false; the reason about the perpendicular bisector is true and is precisely what shows there are infinitely many. C-4.3-LO-2.
Angles in the same segment are equal -- the first clause of C-4.3-LO-6, which is what its concyclicity test is built on.
Proves the same-segment result by halving the same central angle twice, so LO-5's central angle theorem is the engine and LO-6 is the result. Cited to both.
The line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to it -- the converse clause of C-4.3-LO-4, named separately in that outcome.
Defines concyclic and gives the supplementary-opposite-angles test. C-4.3-LO-6's 'tests whether four points are concyclic' clause.
A parallelogram is cyclic only when it is a rectangle, because equal plus supplementary forces 90 degrees. The converse of C-4.3-LO-6 applied as a classification.
False, except for the square: a rhombus's opposite angles are equal but not generally supplementary. The same C-4.3-LO-6 test as qid:706741, in true/false form.
Distance 5 and radius 13 give half-chord 12, so the chord is 24. C-4.3-LO-4's bisection property run in the direction that produces the chord.
A chord through the centre is a diameter, hence twice the radius. Cited to C-4.3-LO-1's chord/diameter definitions rather than LO-4, since no perpendicular distance is involved.
Two chord distances computed by the bisection property, then combined by subtraction or addition depending on which side of the centre they lie. C-4.3-LO-4, with the case analysis being the point.
The SSS congruence proof that equal chords subtend equal angles at the centre. C-4.3-LO-3's forward direction; the converse is the other half of that outcome.
